Arranging 2: Bass and Drums

Why the bass follows the kick, how the groove sets the feel, walking in swing and the tumbao in Latin music.

The bass and drums are the foundation. If they agree, a band can lose everyone else and still sound like a band. This page is about how they agree. How the examples work is explained in the first lesson.

1. The bass follows the kick

The kick drum and the bass are both low and both short at the start of a note. When they land together they sound like one big instrument. When they land apart, the bottom of the band sounds busy and blurred.

Below, the drums play the same pop backbeat throughout. Try each bass line against it. Look at the bass staff and the kick drum (the lowest notes on the drum staff) and see where they line up.

The dotted line is the one the style was written with: the bass plays exactly where the kick plays. The others still work, but they make a different song: roots on every beat is plainer, eighths push harder, root and fifth sounds like country.

2. The drums choose the feel

Now keep the bass line and change the groove. Each one divides the beat differently or puts the backbeat somewhere else.

Half-time moves the snare from 2 and 4 to 3 only: the chords go by just as fast but the song feels half as fast. Arrangers use it for a breakdown or a big final chorus. Four on the floor puts the kick on every beat, which is why the root-eighths bass now sounds like it’s doubling something.

3. Swing: the bass walks, the ride keeps time

In jazz the roles change. The ride cymbal carries the time, the kick drum mostly keeps out of the way, and the bass plays a note on every beat. That’s a walking line: the root on beat 1, other notes of the chord and scale in between, and a note on beat 4 that leads into the next chord.

Compare it with the lighter two-feel (half notes) that a band often plays on the melody before walking for the solos, and with plain chord tones.

4. Latin: the bass anticipates

In son montuno and salsa, the bass plays the tumbao: it doesn’t land on beat 1 at all. The new chord’s root arrives early, on the and of 2 and on 4, and rings over the barline. The clave and congas mark the beat instead.

Switch the congas off, then the drums. With only the bass left, you can hear that it is always a beat ahead of the chord chart.

5. Try it

  • In section 1, play the Root eighths line, then switch the drums to Half-time in section 2. Which bass line would you choose for a half-time chorus?
  • Next: Guitar and keyboards.
